title: Offshore members have contribution pathways
full_text:
Super fund members who have lived overseas or are still currently offshore can access specific deduction strategies even if they have had limited interaction with the retirement savings system, two superannuation specialists have noted.
MLC senior technical service manager Scott Quinn said someone who has spent an extended period overseas and was a non-tax resident during that time could make catch-up contributions on their return.
Quinn gave the example of Beth, who has returned to Australia, has sold an investment property, had a total super balance at 30 June 2026 of less than $500,000 and wants to use catch-up contributions to reduce the tax payable on the realised gain on the investment property.
“She is less than age 67, so we don’t need to worry about the work test, but when we look at MyGov it says she has no carry-forward concessional contributions information to display,” he said during an online technical briefing today.
“She’s been overseas as a non-tax resident for quite a period of time. Can Beth use catch-up concessional contributions?
“Beth can because while you’re a non-tax resident, unused concessional contributions will still accrue and the test time is only in the financial year you want to use the concessional contributions.
“So, if I want to use catch-up concessional contributions in the 2026/27 year, I only need to worry about my total super balance at 30 June 2026. It doesn’t matter what it was before then.
“You also don’t have to have less than $500,000 for it to accrue in a year and you don’t have to be an Australian tax resident for it to accrue either.”
MLC senior technical service manager Chris Chow added Beth could have also made personal deductible contributions while living overseas using the rental income received from the investment property.
“There are considerations around other types of income, but with Australian property that is taxable in Australia you do have rental income,” Chow said.
“So a personal deductible contribution can reduce the income on those amounts and avoid paying foreign resident tax rates as well, which start at the 30 per cent rate from the first dollar, so they can still be useful for that particular purpose.”
